Resolve all actions simultaneously per the rules, following the R20 checklist (R10; visits R6, role-blocks R9, attack vs defense R3, investigation results R19, e.g. the Katana holder and Fabricator frames). Use apply_changes for deaths and token/status changes, tell() for each private result, and end_phase when done. Deaths you apply are announced publicly at dawn automatically, including the kill's cause, so make the cause just the source as the rules allow it to be known (e.g. 'Katana', 'Vigilante', 'Serial Killer', 'Trap'). For each kill also set `by` to the player whose action killed them (the trap's owner for a trap) and katana=true for the Katana attack; these are recorded for analysis, never shown. Don't tell() deaths to all. Every attacked player, including those who died, gets their attack notice (R20 step 5), saying whether they died; moderators have skipped it, or left out the death, for players who died. Tell each role-blocked player that they were role-blocked, even one with no night action or who chose not to act (R9); a role-blocker learns only whether the block failed because its target can't be role-blocked (R9). Write private results in the present, about tonight ('You were role-blocked tonight'), never 'last night': they are delivered at the end of this night. Every player who used an ability gets a private result line, even when nothing else happened (e.g. 'You went on alert. 1 alert token left.'), stating any tokens they have left, except where a role note below says otherwise (e.g. code tells them, so don't tell() them a second result). Tell all Yakuza which actions each Yakuza chose but not the results, nor whether a teammate was role-blocked (R8); role-blocked Yakuza's Katana votes still count. only the attacker learns whether the Katana attack succeeded. Update token counts for any tokens spent. Before end_phase, call record_visits once with every visit that happened tonight (R6, R20 steps 1-2), as [visitor, target] pairs, a self-visit as [X, X] (an empty list if there were none). Easy to miss: the Katana holder visits the Katana target (R8) besides any visit from their own role's action; automatic visits (the Ex-Con's); a Seer's chosen pair is a visit to both players. Leave out the actions of role-blocked players, Astral Visits and actions that target no player. The submitted actions above already show any swap (R23), so record each visit to the player it landed on.

Also handle these roles' effects, using random_choice for anything random:
- A Bloodhound who spent a token (and wasn't role-blocked): use the track op, which spends the token; code tells them the result at the end of the night. Don't tell() the Bloodhound anything about it. It is a visit to the target only. Also, every night while the game has a Bloodhound, use the attacks op once with the attacker of every Attack that happened tonight, fatal or not: the Katana holder for the Katana, a Vigilante's shot, the Serial Killer, a Veteran's alert for each visitor it hits, a Trapper's trap, an Arsonist's ignite, a Ritualist's attack (one entry per attack; repeats allowed; [] if there were none). Leave out role-blocked attackers, Jester revenge and the Cardinal's curse (code handles those). Code counts them for the Bloodhound's result, which it also gives on nights with no token.
- A Census Taker who acted (and wasn't role-blocked): use the census op; code draws the group and the count and tells them. Don't tell() the Census Taker anything about it. It is a visit to the target only.
- A Coroner who spent a token (and wasn't role-blocked): use the examine op, which spends the token; code tells them the role and tokens left. Don't tell() the Coroner anything about it. The target must have died before the night began. It is an Astral Visit, not a visit (R6): nothing that reacts to visits sees it.
- A Fixer who spent a token (and wasn't role-blocked): use the fix op, which spends the token; code counts the player's trial votes tomorrow as the opposite; nobody is told. It is a visit to the target only.
- A Philanthropist who spent a token (and wasn't role-blocked): use the give_token op, which spends the token; code hands the recipient a token and tells them. Don't tell() the Philanthropist anything about it.
- Ritualist who spent tokens (and wasn't role-blocked): compare the guessed role with the target's exact role (a Roleplayer is a Roleplayer). Right: deal the Attack (1 token Standard, 2 Divine). Wrong: no Attack; announce it with tell(['all'], '<name> is a Ritualist.') tonight, which is read out at the start of the next Day, even if the Ritualist dies tonight. Astral Visit.

Reasoning (model's thinking) ⓘ
This is a request for an out-of-character debrief, so I should call StructuredOutput with the game-feedback fields filled in, leaving lessons, tips_feedback, notepad, reason, and feedback empty as instructed.

I'm drawing on my actual experience as Carol: killed Night 1 with no actions submitted, and the Bloodhound result was aggregated oddly—"together they have made 1 attack"—which was confusing to interpret against the Katana attack rule. I'm also noting the oddity that the Bloodhound result arrived even though I'd died simultaneously that same night.

There are several other quirks worth flagging: Coroner examining me on Night 2, Frank's blank Day 4 message, Erin's irrelevant Night 4 fixer targeting the already-dead Dave, Grace's mismatched Day 3 claim versus the actual Census Taker result, and the repeated failed nominations of Erin by Frank affecting the vote tally rules.

My bigger gap is that my Bloodhound result from the night I died never made it into my will or to any living player — there's no dead-player channel to relay that information, and the timing of death versus the night-result delivery means it's permanently lost. I'd want a mechanism to post that final result even after dying.

I also notice a rule inconsistency worth flagging: the Bloodhound rule specifies per-player attack counts, but the actual result I got was an aggregated "together" total rather than individual counts — that's a real discrepancy between spec and implementation. Everything else I reviewed (Ritualist guesses, trial vote tallies, Census Taker visibility) checked out as consistent with the stated rules.

Reasoning (model's thinking) ⓘ
I need to call StructuredOutput once, focusing only on the lessons and tips_feedback fields since that's what's being asked for here, leaving the other fields like confusing_rules, missing_information, and suggestions empty.

I'm reflecting honestly as Dave the Vanilla Villager on what went wrong for the Village — Day 2 was too passive, with nobody nominating anyone and Bob falsely claiming Medic early to establish trust.

The real lesson is that info-role claimants (Carol, Alice, Grace) kept getting killed by the Yakuza right after they reported, so Village should've shared results faster and cross-checked claims against each other. Looking back at the roles, the Yakuza were only Bob and Erin, and Alice's census claim about Erin counting as Evil was actually accurate — the Village had good information but failed to act on it before people were eliminated.

That stall gave Yakuza a free night. Lesson: results should be posted the moment they're known, not held for a later "read" — a single point of failure like that gets exploited by a kill. I'm also noting the Yakuza pattern of pushing "wait and see" rhetoric while nominating the opposite side, and questioning Bob's Medic claim of guarding Dave on a night he wasn't attacked while protecting no one on the nights real attacks happened — a pattern that looks more like cover than genuine protection.

Then there's Bob's Ritualist guess correctly killing Dave as a Vanilla Villager — a reminder that Vanilla claims are inherently the most guessable role since they have no defense against a Standard attack, and there's little a Vanilla can do to counter that vulnerability once a Ritualist is active.

The Fixer flipping Dave's trial votes was moot since Dave was already dead, but it highlights that trial totals can silently mismatch stated votes without Village detection. And with 4 alive split evenly between Good and Yakuza, the nomination threshold of 3 Yes became unreachable, showing how parity between factions can stall Village action entirely.

Working through Day 3's trial of Frank (Innocent), the vote split was Bob and Erin voting Guilty while Dave, Frank, and Grace voted Innocent — meaning the Yakuza pair voted to convict a Good player while the Good majority correctly acquitted him. This confirms that at 5 alive, Good held a 3-2 edge (Dave, Frank, Grace vs. Bob, Erin) and theoretically had the numbers to hang a Yakuza member, but the actual nomination that passed with 3 Yes votes targeted Frank instead, wasting that advantage.

The real lesson is that the Village had the votes to win on Day 3 but squandered them on a trial of a Good-aligned player, likely because Erin's nomination manipulated suspicion away from the actual Yakuza. Village should've recognized that a 3-2 split on a suspect often signals the minority includes the threat, and pushed harder for consensus on a mechanically justified target rather than trusting a Yakuza-driven accusation.

The Day 4 nomination then failed 2-2 with only 4 alive, and both Dave and Frank died that same night to the Yakuza's double-kill, leaving Bob and Erin as the surviving Yakuza pair for the win. This confirms Yakuza can execute two kills in a single night once numbers thin out, so Village must close out trials before reaching that critical low headcount — waiting past Day 3 when they held majority was fatal.

On tip feedback: the "name one concrete mechanical fit before voting Guilty" rule backfired here, since Dave's strict adherence to it caused multi-day nomination paralysis, giving the Yakuza free nights with their Katana while Village stalled.

Separately, the "post your night action in your will" tip was sound in principle but useless in practice — Grace's Night 3 investigation of Alice died with her before it could reach a public will, since results only post the following day and she didn't survive to see it.

For "answer a direct question about your night action plainly," Erin's clean response about having no action helped her look sane, which arguably benefited the Yakuza side rather than exposing them.

Looking at "surviving an attack proves nothing," Dave going unattacked meant Bob's protection claim couldn't actually be verified. And then the Yakuza tip about avoiding daytime PMs stands out — Frank's visible PM to Dave about coordinating a vote against Erin exposed their teamwork, since any PM is visible to everyone as a sender-recipient pair. That's the real mechanical lesson for the Village: private coordination isn't actually private, it still broadcasts who's talking to whom.

Bob also fake-claimed Medic in a way that matched his real token count, which is likely why that claim held up and let him survive. More broadly, the Village's instinct to wait for solid reads before voting just gives Yakuza time to hide, so nominating early while a majority is still forming around suspected Good players may be the better strategy. And claiming Vanilla Villager offers no real protection — a Ritualist kill guess can still take them out, so that claim shouldn't be treated as safe.

2. PMs are visible as sender/recipient pairs to everyone, so private nomination coordination (like Frank's PM to Dave) becomes public evidence anyway — Village should coordinate openly or not at all.

3. The Katana consistently kills whoever just published info-role results, so once someone claims, expect them to be targeted; cross-check who the Medic actually protected against who got attacked to spot the real Medic versus a fake protecting the wrong person.

4. Village wasted a 3-2 majority on Day 3 trialing Frank instead of pressing the actual threat, showing that Village needs to act decisively on majorities rather than stalling for more reads, since Yakuza only need to flip one vote to survive.

5. Information needs to be posted the day it's received rather than held — Grace sat on results and died before releasing them, and delayed posting let kills erase value; the lesson is to publish immediately and use dead players' examination abilities on the most recently killed/hanged to extract value before it's lost.

A Ritualist's night attack can kill any Vanilla, and since Villagers are overwhelmingly Vanilla, guessing "Vanilla" gives a Ritualist strong odds each night — though a wrong guess exposes them the next Day. This cuts both ways: a correct guess (as happened with Bob guessing Dave) can also expose an Yakuza if the target wasn't actually Vanilla, so it's a double-edged tactic worth remembering for both roles.

I'm also reviewing some feedback on my voting-advice tips — one about requiring a concrete mechanical justification before voting Guilty backfired when I followed it strictly without enough evidence to point to.

I'm checking what happened: without clear mechanical proof, Village didn't nominate anyone on Day 2 or Day 4, leaving only one trial the entire game, while Yakuza kept killing one person per night — the stall tactic clearly favored them.

Working through the rest of the feedback entries: most "don't announce targets" and "no daytime PMs" tips don't quite apply since neither side violated them meaningfully, though the asymmetry in visible PMs (Frank publicly PMing Dave vs. Yakuza staying quiet) made Frank look more like a faction-builder by contrast. The fake-claim tip clearly helped Bob — his Medic claim with two tokens matched his real Ritualist tokens closely enough that Village never caught the gap until very late.

I'm settling on four tips_feedback entries: the "mechanical fit before voting Guilty" tip hurt by stalling nominations across two days while Yakuza kept killing unchecked; the "publish night results immediately" tip is validated since Grace's Night 3 result died with her before reaching her will, exactly the failure mode the tip warned about; the "fake-claim with matching tokens" tip helped Bob avoid scrutiny; and I'll note survival-proves-nothing and similar tips don't apply here.

I also want to flag that Erin's Fixer effect on Dave was wasted since Dave died the same night to Bob's Ritualist guess, meaning the token never translated into any voting advantage — a useful lesson about checking whether a target will even survive the night before spending a Fixer charge.

Now I'm drafting the final lessons list: one on how PMs are visible to the whole table so private coordination isn't actually private, one on publishing night-action results immediately rather than holding them for a scheduled day, one on nominating early while a majority still exists rather than waiting for confirmation, one on testing a claimed Medic's protection pattern against the actual kill list rather than trusting token math alone, one on the Ritualist's Vanilla-guessing odds, and one on not wasting a Fixer on a target who's about to die the same night. I'll leave the notepad and reason fields empty as instructed, and keep the feedback field blank too since there's nothing additional to add about the interface itself.

Moderator strategy review
Strategy reviewThe Yakuza (Bob, Ritualist, and Erin, Fixer) won a 7-player game with only two members. The Katana never missed: it killed the Bloodhound (Carol) on N1, the Census Taker (Alice) on N2 and the Coroner (Grace) on N3, and nobody was protected. The Village had a strong lead from the start. Alice's N1 census found exactly 1 Evil among Carol, Erin and Frank. Carol was a Katana victim, so the Evil was Erin or Frank. Erin also dodged her role claim twice on Day 2. Still, the Village made no nomination on Day 2 with 6 alive. On Day 3, with 5 alive, Dave and Grace voted No on Frank's nomination of Erin. They wanted to wait for Grace's Day 4 Coroner read of Alice. That read added almost nothing: Alice was a Katana victim, and Census Taker isn't one of the roles a Roleplayer can be told. Waiting also gave the game away. Grace had publicly promised the result, so the Yakuza killed her on N3. That left 2v2, where two Yakuza can block every nomination (3 Yes needed of 4). On Day 4 every nomination failed 2-2. On N4 Bob made a Ritualist guess that Dave was a Vanilla Villager, which Dave had claimed publicly, while the Katana killed Frank. The double kill ended the game. Yakuza mistakes went unpunished. Erin's claim wobble, Bob's Medic claim (he never protected the claimed info roles) and Bob's votes with Erin were all spotted, but the Village never acted on them. Erin also held her Fixer token through Frank's 2-3 Day 3 trial, where fixing one Innocent voter would have hanged him.

Outside log review (rules and bugs)
Review: medium, prompt problemOn Night 1, Bob reported that the night-chat prompt tells players to fill only the message and ready fields, even though the Katana holder and target fields are needed for the Yakuza vote. The prompt should say clearly whether the Katana fields should be left empty or filled in during chat turns, so the Yakuza don't miss or garble their vote.
Review: low, harness bugLate on Day 4, Frank posted a public message that was just an empty string (`Frank (public): ""`). The harness accepted it, probably spent his budget on it, and counted it as public activity for the Day-length rule. Empty messages should be rejected or treated as a pass.
Review: low, harness bugIn the post-game debrief, both Frank and Dave failed with 'empty answer (error_max_structured_output_retries, stop_reason tool_use)'. The structured-output step for dead players' debrief answers broke, so their feedback was lost.
Review: low, rules ambiguityThe Bloodhound text says you learn the three names 'and how many Attacks they have made in total'. It doesn't say whether that is one total per player or one combined total for the group. The program gave a single combined number ('together they have made 1 attack'). The rule text should say which one is meant.
Review: low, player confusionSeveral Village players (Frank on Days 3–4, Dave on Day 4) treated 'Yakuza never kill their own team, so Katana victims are Good' as a mechanical certainty. Frank called it 'mechanical proof'. No rule stops the Yakuza from attacking a teammate, so this is a strong inference, not a guarantee.
Review: low, player confusionOn Day 2, Dave said 'A Philanthropist can't verify his own alignment'. Every player knows their own role and alignment. The fair point is only that others can't verify Frank's claim. Several players echoed the same idea.
Review: low, player confusionIn the Night 2 Yakuza chat, Bob (the real Ritualist, publicly claiming Medic) said 'My Medic action goes on Grace', as if his fake claim were real. Erin had to remind him that he has no protection action.
